podcast.title: C81 Predecessor (1981)
podcast.body: In 1981, the NME had previously attempted to assert its influence with a cassette compilation called *C81*, which achieved modest success. This earlier effort set a precedent for their more impactful *C86* project, demonstrating the tabloid's ongoing commitment to discovering and championing new musical talent. "The NME had tried to seize the lead once before 1981, with a cassette called C81, and that had been a modest success."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: C86 Compilation (May 1986)
podcast.body: As one of the UK's prominent weekly music tabloids, the NME offered its readers a landmark compilation cassette titled *C86* in May 1986. This cassette, whose name referenced both tape length conventions and its release year, became a pivotal moment—a "big bang"—for the British indie scene by showcasing guitar-based indie songs and playing a crucial role in the discovery and promotion of new music. "In May 1986, the NME, the new musical express, one of the UK's weekly music tabloids, hadn't offered for their readers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "And the Motorcade Sped On" Giveaway (February 1987)
podcast.body: The music magazine NME gave away Steinsky and Mass Media's song "And the Motorcade Sped On" with an issue in February 1987. "It was given away with an issue of the NME in February 1987."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Widespread Adoption of "Britpop" (January 1995)
podcast.body: The term "Britpop" reached its "real tipping point" in an issue of *NME* in January 1995, after which it became widely adopted by everyone to describe the burgeoning British music scene. "But the real tipping point seemed to come in an issue of the NME in January 1995. And after that, everybody began to use Brit Pop to describe what was going on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Crucial Role in British Music Discovery
podcast.body: During a period when the British public had limited access to new music on the state-run BBC radio, weekly music tabloids like the NME, along with three other competing publications, became essential for discovering and promoting new bands. These papers played a critical role in anointing the "next big thing" and shaping the musical landscape. "At the time, there were four music tabloids, and because the British public was stuck mainly with the state BBC, there wasn't a lot of new music played on the radio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: High Rating for Arctic Monkeys' AM
podcast.body: The NME magazine awarded the Arctic Monkeys' "AM" album a perfect 10 out of 10 rating. This high score reflects the critical acclaim the album received in Europe, positioning it as one of the band's best works. "La propia revista NEM y el Rino Nido le daban 10 sobre 10."

podcast.title: NME's Role in Britpop
podcast.body: The weekly music paper NME, along with Melody Maker, devoted significant coverage to the emerging Britpop scene, helping to establish it as a "new and very viable local music scene." "And the weekly papers, the NME and Melodymaker, some thirtieth into what appeared to be a new and very viable local music scene."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Role in British Music Press
podcast.body: NME was one of the numerous British music magazines and tabloids that filled the void left by the limited legal commercial radio in Britain prior to the 1970s. These publications saw it as their duty to discover and hype new music and scenes. "The NME, sounds, melody maker, and dozens more filled the gap played by radio in North America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
